title: What is a write blocker?
quick: A write blocker is a hardware device or software setting that lets a computer read a storage device but stops commands that would change it, so the original evidence is not altered during copying.

sections.title: The problem it solves
text: Operating systems often write to a drive that is just plugged in. Windows may add hidden folders and index data. Some systems try to repair a file system or update access times. These small changes alter the original and make it harder to prove it is unchanged.
A write blocker is placed between the evidence drive and the examiner's computer so that such writes never reach the drive.

sections.title: What it passes and what it stops
text: Computers talk to a drive using commands. Commands that only read data or ask for information are passed through. Commands that would change the data are blocked. NIST publishes a specification for hardware write blockers, and tests devices against it through its CFTT program.
points: Blocked: commands that modify the protected drive.
Passed: read commands and information commands.
The reply from the drive should reach the computer unchanged.
Some devices have a switch for protected and unprotected mode, or lights to show the state.

sections.title: Using one in practice
text: Connect the blocker to the examiner computer first, then connect the evidence drive. Check that the drive is shown as read-only. Record the blocker model, serial number and firmware version, plus the date and time. Create the image, then compare hash values. Test the blocker on a spare drive before casework and repeat tests on a routine schedule, as your lab requires.

sections.title: What a blocker does not do
text: It does not make a copy and it does not check hashes. It also does not protect against a drive that is already failing. Many phones are not simple disks, so a normal disk write blocker does not apply to them. Other methods are used, and they are covered in the mobile topics.

example: An examiner needs to image a SATA drive from a desktop. She connects a hardware write blocker to her workstation, then attaches the drive. The workstation shows the disk as read-only. She notes the blocker serial number, images the drive and checks that the image hash matches the source hash.
mistakes: Connecting the evidence drive before the blocker is attached and switched on.
Never testing the blocker, or testing it only once.
Treating a read-only file system view as full write blocking.
Forgetting to log the model, serial number and firmware.
Expecting a disk blocker to work for a phone.

terms.meaning: Stopping write commands from reaching a storage device.
A state where data can be read but not changed.
The evidence drive that sits behind the blocker.
The small built-in program that runs a device such as a blocker.
The NIST Computer Forensics Tool Testing program, which publishes specifications and test results.

exam.q: What must a write blocker do?
exam.a: Block commands that change the protected drive, and pass commands that only read or request information, with the replies unchanged.

exam.q: In what order do you connect the devices?
exam.a: Attach the blocker to the examiner computer first, confirm it is working, then connect the evidence drive. Follow your lab's procedure.

exam.q: How do you know your blocker works?
exam.a: Test it on a spare drive and keep the test record. Also use published test results as a guide, but still test your own unit.
